> resultcox = inla(formula, family = "coxph", data = sim.data,
> control.hazard=list(model="rw1",cutpoints=cutpoints))

you'll need here to put a proper prior on the intercept as it interacts
with the rw-model for the baseline harazard (although its constrained to
sum to zero). default is prec.intercept = 0, which can cause trouble
sometimes.

here is the updated example. I also disovered a minor error in the plot
due to a previous name-change, which I have fixed, so you need to do

	inla.upgrade(testing=TRUE)

first, before plotting the results.

***************

sim.data = read.csv("data.csv")

## cutpoints need to cover the range of the data
cutpoints = c(0, 1, 4.33, 26, 53)

formula = inla.surv(t, occ) ~ period

resultcox = inla(formula, family = "coxph", data = sim.data,  verbose=T,
        control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0.001))

resultcox = inla(formula, family = "coxph", data = sim.data,

        control.fixed = list(prec.intercept = 0.001),
        control.hazard=list(model="rw1",cutpoints=cutpoints))

messages.subject: Creating a mesh on a sphere S2
messages.subject_clean: Creating a mesh on a sphere S2
messages.body_plain:
Hi!
The code currently only supports calculating spherical harmonics on a proper spherical mesh. For global models, the intended usage is to build meshes that live on the curved space, so that distances and connectivity are correct. Long-lat coordinates are usually very inappropriate, unless the study region is very local, and close to the equator.  To build a such a mesh, simply convert Lon-lat to Cartesian xyz and supply that to inla.mesh.create.

That being said, the following workaround can be used if you really need o calculate spherical harmonics in Lon-lat in R2:
1. Create your flat mesh.
2. Create another mesh,call it mesh2, on the sphere, as described above, using the mesh points mesh$loc from step 1., and refine=false.
3. Calculate sph.harm on mesh2, and index by mesh2$idx$loc to get the values for the flat mesh.

More documentation for all this is on its way.

Finn L

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Code for Laplace prior
messages.body_plain:
The prior specification is correct, but it will not do what you want.

I am assuming that you wish to fit the Bayesian Lasso model

y|beta,sigma ~ X*beta + eps
beta_j|sigma ~ Laplace( beta_j; mean=0, scale=sigma^2)

This cannot be fitted in INLA because the beta's are not Gaussian.

To do this in INLA, you need to use the Hierarchical model specification

Assume that there are p beta's. Then

y|beta,sigma ~ N(X*beta, sigma^2 *I)
beta|sigma, tau_1,..., tau_p ~ N(0_p, sigma^2 * D_p)
where D_p = diag(tau_1^2, ..., tau_p^2)
p(tau_j) = lambda^2/2*exp(-lambda^2*tau_j^2/2

So the prior that you need to set is just normally distributed with
variance lambda.  You cannot put a prior on lambda within the INLA
framework.

As said in a previous email, you cannot have p > 10 (15 at the
absolute maximum).

I hope this helps,

Dan

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, 2012-07-27 at 07:10 -0700, Elias T. Krainski wrote:
> Let the model with linear predictor
>       \alpha_j + s_i*\beta_j,   s_i is a latent model.
> I use INLA to fit \beta_j using copy strategy.
> But I have an expressive number of \beta_j.
> It is possible to fit \beta_j such as fixed effect?
> Or another latent model?

would it be better if you could express the linear predictor as

	A %*% a + S %*% s

where 'a' and 's' are vectors of fixed effects, and A and S two
matrices ?

INLA support this format,

	formula = y ~ -1 + A + S

where A and S are matrices.

would this help?

the names of the fixed effects are taken from the appropriate names of
the matrices, with the variable name as the prefix.

here is a small example:

        n = 100

        n.a = 3
        A = matrix(runif(n*n.a), n, n.a)
        a = rnorm(n.a)

        n.s = 5
        S = matrix(runif(n*n.s), n, n.s)
        s = rnorm(n.s)

        y = 0 + A %*% a + S %*% s + rnorm(n, sd = 0.01)
        formula = y ~ -1 + A + S
        r = inla(formula,  data = list(y=y,  A=A,  S=S))
        summary(r)

        print(paste("error", sum(abs(r$summary.fixed[,"mean"] -
        c(a,s)))))

messages.body_plain:
I have a latent model z. It is replicated m times multiplied by constant b[j], j=1, 2, ..., m. So, variance of z changes m times. I think that b[j] can be estimated using copy strategy.

Let me clarify with an example:

n <- 100; m <- 5
a <- 3*(m:1/m); b <- 1:m/m

j <- rep(1:m, each=n)
x <- rep(rnorm(n), m)*b[j]
y <- rpois(n*m, exp(a[j] + x))

tapply(x, b[j], sd)
tapply(y, a[j], mean)

formula <- update(y ~ 0 + j + f(i, wi, model="iid", initial=0, fixed=TRUE),
                  paste(".~.+", paste('f(i.',1:m,', w.',1:m,
                                      ", copy='i', fixed=FALSE)",
                                      sep="", collapse="+")))

dat <- data.frame(y=y, j=factor(j), i=rep(1:n,m), wi=rep(0,n*m),
                  i=kronecker(matrix(1,m,m), 1:n),
                  w=kronecker(diag(m),rep(1,n)))

require(INLA)
res <- inla(formula, data=dat, family="poisson")
cbind(true=a, res$summary.fix)
cbind(true=b, res$summary.hyperpar)

It is possible to fit b[j] without specify it such as hyperparameter?

All the best!
Elias T. Krainski

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 2012-07-30 at 01:45 -0700, cck wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I was running a spatial model but when it's just about to complete I
> got the error below.
>
> MAPKIT: ERROR: malloc failed (hash.c, line 1330)
> MAPKIT: ERROR: malloc failed (hash.c, line 1330)
>
> Could this be related to limited memory in my computer?

yes. the hash-library fail to get more memory. this is what you can do

-  restart your computer  (release used memory)
-  reduce the models-size
-  buy more ram
-  run it on another computer with more ram
-  run it using fewer threads, with

	inla.setOption(num.threads=1)
	r = inla(...)

   f.ex, which only uses 1 'cpu' instead of all available. this helps
because a lot of the internal storage is duplicated for each thread.
(you got two errors above, most likely, one for each of the two
threads).

--
